caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 595 of 1963
lawyer:
Shahabuddin Ahmed with A. Halim—For the appellant.
B. N. Chowdhury—For the respondent.
parties:
Meherjan Bibi ------- Appellant
Vs.
Naimuddin Dhali being dead, one of his heirs: Raisuddin Dhali and others ------- Respondents
case_source: Appeal against the decree of Mr. Anisuddin Ahmed, Additional District Judge 3rd Court of Zilla Mymensingh.
full_judgment:
The plaintiff obtained a preliminary decree in the trial Court for petition of the mil land against the defendant No. 32 on content with costs and expert against the rest. On appeal by the defendant No. 32 the appeal was allowed and the decree of the trial Court was modified. The plaintiff the appellant in this Second Appeal.

2. The plaintiff's case shortly is that the suit lands originally belonged to Adam Munshi, Adam Munshi died leaving a son Ismail and three daughters; Bajiterma, Hakimerma, and Kaluarma as his heirs, Ismail left two sons Bulurbap and Asmat, a daughter Meherjan Bibi (plaintiff) and a widow Pirjan as his heirs. Next to die wee Bulurbap who left as a widow Tearma mother Pirjan brother Asmat and sister plaintiff. Pirjan died next leaving a son Asmat and daughter plaintiff Asmat also died leaving defendant. 4 as Tearma died leaving defendants 6-9 an heirs Defendants 10 and 11 are the heirs of Bajiterma, Defendants 12-16 are heirs of Hakimerma who is also dead. Kaluarma died leaving defendants 17-23 as heirs. Defendants 24-29 are heirs of Kaliarma, who is one of the daughters of Kaliarma. Other defendants including the contesting defendant No. 32 are purchasers from the original owners. Defendant No. 32 agreeing with the gemology only asserts that the original owner of the suit land was Sada Dhali who died leaving a son Adam Munshi, and 2 daughters Elemjan and Afarjan Into consideration the plaintiff's share in the suit land stands reduced, according to the defendant No. 32.

3. The undisputed position in the case is that if Adam Munshi Is found to be the original owner the plaintiff's claim to the suit land becomes to 2.11.3-1.4/5th kranti as decreed by the trial Court but if Sada Dali is found to be the original owner the plaintiff's share comes to 1.8 3-1/2 kranti as decreed by the appellate Court below.

4. At the trial of the suit the plaintiff produced C S. Khatian Est. 1 showing that the suit land wan recorded in the name of Adam Munshi alone. It also shows that one Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord of the suit land. The concealing defendant No. 32 produced two Chittas Exts. B and B(I) prepared in 1883 in a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and one Amal Prasanna Bal and other by an Amin of the Collectorate in connection with partition of Touzi No 115 under the Estate Partition Act. The trial Court held that only parts of the suit land are covered by Chitta Dags in some of which Sada Dhali were found to be in possession with Abbas Dhali and in some with others. Only in some of the Chitta Dags, Sada Dhali was found to be in exclusive possession. The Trial Court held that under no circumstance could it be said that the suit land in their entirely belonged to Sada Dhali at any time; There were other interested persons also. Apparently, the trial Court held, three were great changes in possession.

4A. The appellate Court Into observed that the plaintiff has not stated how Adam Munshi acquired the suit land. It analysed the evidence of the Pleader Commissioner who was appointed to relay the Chitta Dags with C. S. P plots in suit. Suit land contained 12 C S plot. Out of 12 plots the defendant has not furnished Chitta papers of 2 plots for repayment 2 C. S. plots are fully attracted by the Chitta Dags, The remaining 8 C. S. plots are pertly attracted by the Chitta Dags. The appellate Court below finds that 10 suit plot are 'substantially' attracted by Chitta Dags. As the plaintiff flied no basic document to show that the remaining 2 C S. plots were self-acquired properties of Adam Munshi, it held that these plots also were in possession of Sada Dhali. It came to the conclusion that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land.

5. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contended that the appellate Court below erred in coming to finding that Sada Dhali was the owner at the time of  reparation of CS record without there being any evidence on record to that effect. It erred in law in relying upon the Ext. B and B(I) which have got no relevance at all to the facts and circumstances of the case. Ext. 1 the CS khatian which was prepared some time in 1910 or 1911 shows that Jogesh Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord and Adam Munshi alone was in possession of the suit land. Exts. B and B(I) were prepared in 1883 ie. about 30 years before the C. S. operation. In a case between one Uma Sundar Debya and Kamal Prosonna Bal and others. The defendant adduced no evidence to show that Jogesh Chakraborty was in any way connected with either Uma Sundar Debya or Kamal Prosonna Bal, Sada Dhali might have been in possession of some suit plots in 1893 under a different landlord but in the meanwhile with in the course of 30 years the superior landlord of the suit land changed and with the change of the landlord tenants also changed. There is no evidence at all that Sada Dhali continued to be in possession of the entire suit land for the next 30 years. Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed submits that no evidence having been adduced by the defendant as to what happened in the meanwhile the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights stand unrebutted.

6.. Mr. B. N. Choudhury, the learned advocate for the respondent, has contended that the question whether the presumption as to correctness of entry in the record of rights has been rebutted or not is a question of fact and however erroneously the appellate Court below might have come to that finding of fact, it cannot be interfered with In a second appeal. He had cited several decisions to that effect.

7. In a case where the plaintiff relies upon the entry in the record of rights for the basis of his title it is not necessary for him to show the basis of his title of the entry in the record or right. As was held in the case of Alamuddin Munshi and others vs. Mainuddin Talukder and others reported in 14 D.L.R. 725.

"Merely because there Is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of rights, the presumption is not rebutted to view of the provision of section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and also the procedure as laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the other concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the entries are incorrect. The absence of evidence for the basis of the entries may be a circumstance which along with other evidence may go to show that the presumption has been rebutted”.

<u>8. Yet, the appellate Court below merely because the plaintiff failed to produce any basis of the C.S Khatian held that Sada Dhali was in possession of at least 2 C.S. plots in respect of which the defendant did not file any Chitta papers. This finding cannot be sustained. For it is well settled, as has been held in the case of Aminuddin Biswas Vs, Miajan Biswas, reported in 12 D L R. 103. 'The presumption of correctness, as available on the strength of section 103 B (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it.". There was no evidence at all in respect of the said 2 plots that Sada Dhali was in possession even in 1883. In respect of the 10 remaining suit plots the appellate Court below in common with the trial Court held that in some plots Sada Dhali is found to be in exclusive possession and in some other plots he is found to be in Joint possession with Abbas Dhali and others. While the trial Court held that apparently there were great change in possession after the Chitta Dags were prepared, the appellate Court below without any further evidence on record came to hold that Sada Dhali was the owner of the entire suit land. It is no doubt well settled, contended by Mr B.N. Chowdhury that where evidence was led in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights and the appellate Court below comes to a finding that the preemption stands rebutted, that finding is final and cannot be interfered with in the second appellate jurisdiction. In all the decisions cited before me, namely, the case of Wali Mohammad and others Vs. Mohammad Bakhsh, reported in 51 C.L J. 518 Ghulam Mohammad Vs. Secretary of State reported in A.I.R 1938 (L) 445-and Charu Bala Rudra Vs. Narayan Prasad Sen reported in 14 DLR 159 the presumption was rebutted on the basis of relevant evidence on record. In the present case, however, the defendant had not adduced any evidence at all as to what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of C S. records or approximately earlier to that Mr. B N. Chowdhury submits that by producing Exts. B and B (I) the defendant has discharged the onus of proving that CS khatian has no basis. Thereafter, he argue, it is for the plaintiff to show that her predecessor in interest was in possession of the suit land at the relevant lime. It is difficult to agree with Mr. B.N Chowdhury. By adducing evidence of certain state of affairs 30 years back, how can it be said that the basis of C.S. khatian has been shaken? All that the attendant has produced in this case in the state of affairs relating to 10 out of 82 suit plots as far back as in 1883 which shows superior ownership and possession in the names of a different set of persons. How that evidence is evidence at all in rebuttal of the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights is difficult to appreciate. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has failed to cite a tingle decision to show that evidence of such remote chamber has any bearing upon the presumption of correctness of entry in the record of rights. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed has cited the case of Maurabgi Tewari Vs. Kanhaiya Tewari reported In 123 IC 390 in support of his contention that when Chitta Dags and C.S. record show plan of two different persons it must be presumption that at some time between the two periods the person recorded In in the Chitta Dags lost their possession and that the person whose name appears in the C.S. khatian obtained possession, although there Is no presumption regarding the exact time at which the change of affairs took place. I entirely agree with the ratio decidendi of that decision.</u>

<u>While the trial Court rightly held that apparently were great changes in possession. In the meanwhile, the mining link in between the slate of affairs in 1883 and the C.S operation In 1910 or 1911 has been filled up by the appellate Court below by conjectures and surmises. It surmised that there was a division or partition for convenience of pollution between Sada Dhali and Abbas Dhali. It conjectured that an excess area of .04 acre in C.S. plot Nos 1088 might have accrued due to encroachment on adjoining laud and it also surmised as to how the suit property devolved relying upon a stray observation of P W. 4.</u>

<u>In such circumstances the finding of the appellate Court below that Sada Dhali was the owner of the suit land cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>In the result, the appeal is the judgment and decree of the Court below are set aside and those of the trial are restored.</u>

<u>There will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.
